title: Rethinking Input Complexity in Transformer-Based Clinical Prediction: Implications for Feature Dimensionality and Sequence Length in Longitudinal EHR Data
abstract: Objective: Transformer-based models for clinical prediction using longitudinal electronic health record (EHR) data are often developed with large feature sets and long patient histories under the assumption that more data improves performance. However, high-dimensional inputs and long sequences increase computational burden, potentially limiting scalability. We evaluated how feature dimensionality and sequence length affect predictive performance, calibration, risk stratification, and computational efficiency in EHR prediction. Methods: Using longitudinal EHR data from adults with mild asthma in an integrated healthcare system, we evaluated input representation design for predicting acute asthma exacerbation. Feature dimensionality was reduced using Integrated Gradients attribution scores, univariate performance-based selection, and clinically guided selection strategies. Sequence length was varied using percentile-based truncation of patient histories. Performance was assessed using discrimination, calibration, high-risk classification, threshold-based event capture, and computational efficiency across regions. Results: Models using fewer features achieved discrimination comparable to the 80-feature reference model, with AUROC values ranging from 0.843 to 0.864 versus 0.870 for the full model. Moderate sequence-length truncation reduced training time by more than 70% with minimal loss in discrimination. Although reduced-dimensional models showed attenuation of predicted risk at the upper tail, they identified similar high-risk populations and captured comparable proportions of asthma exacerbation events at clinically relevant thresholds. Conclusion: Transformer-based prediction models maintained strong performance across reduced feature sets. While dimensionality reduction modestly affected calibration at the highest risk levels, moderate sequence-length reduction substantially reduced computational burden with limited change in overall discrimination. These findings highlight trade-offs between input complexity, predictive performance, and computational efficiency. Funding: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, National Institutes of Health (R01 HL163049). Lay Summary: Artificial intelligence models are increasingly used to predict clinical outcomes from electronic health record (EHR) data. Many modern deep learning models are built using large numbers of clinical variables and long patient histories because more data is often assumed to improve prediction. However, these complex models require substantial computing resources and may be difficult to implement in real-world healthcare systems.In this study, we examined whether simpler input designs could maintain strong predictive performance while reducing computational burden. Using transformer-based models and longitudinal EHR data from adults with mild asthma, we systematically evaluated how the number of clinical features and the length of patient histories affected prediction performance and efficiency.We found that models using fewer features and shorter patient histories performed similarly to more complex models for identifying patients at high risk of acute asthma exacerbation. Although simplified models showed modest differences in predicted risk estimates at the highest risk levels, they identified similar high-risk patient groups and captured similar numbers of asthma exacerbation events.These findings suggest that deep learning models for healthcare prediction may not require highly complex input designs to achieve clinically useful performance, which could improve scalability and real-world implementation.

title: Laundering the Quantum Horizon: How Category Drift, Metric Substitution and Circular Validation Sustain the Appearance of a Forecastable Quantum Market
abstract: It has become fashionable among quantum sceptics to argue that quantum technologies are irrelevant to near-term commercial applications because the timeline for achieving practical quantum advantage continuously slips. In response, quantum proponents and, in particular, multinational advisory firms can adopt the opposite extreme, presenting high-end market forecasts as evidence of momentum. Regardless of the underlying motivations on either side, both positions lack the analytical rigor necessary to forecast the trajectory of a complex, emerging technology ecosystem. In this paper, we bring the conversation back to its core questions: What metrics are currently used to evaluate and forecast the quantum technology market, and what are the structural consequences of using them? Our objective is not to critique the ethics of specific organizations, but rather to interrogate the opaque methodologies behind these headline figures and examine the systemic risks this narrative mechanism poses to the long-term sustainability of the quantum ecosystem.

title: Title: Dynamically Generated Prime Number Sequences via Quantum Simulation
abstract: The quest for prime numbers remains a fundamental challenge in mathematics, driving a persistent desire for more efficient prime number generation techniques. Classical methods often struggle to produce sufficient numbers, while the search for novel prime distribution patterns is a long-standing endeavor. This paper explores a novel approach utilizing quantum simulation to generate and analyze prime number sequences with significantly enhanced density. We propose a quantum simulation technique that leverages quantum entanglement to create a highly complex, multi-scale model of prime number distribution. This model allows for the identification of intricate patterns and distributions, far exceeding the capabilities of classical computation. We detail the theoretical framework, the quantum algorithm implementation, and preliminary results demonstrating a substantial increase in prime number density compared to existing methods. This advancement holds the potential to revolutionize prime number discovery and contribute to a deeper understanding of the fundamental properties of prime numbers.

title: Quantum Entanglement Neural Networks: A Probabilistic Approach
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a bizarre phenomenon in quantum mechanics, presents a novel approach to neural network training. This paper explores the potential of leveraging entanglement to enhance the efficiency and adaptability of neural networks, specifically focusing on reducing computational errors and enabling more effective parameter adjustment. We propose a novel network architecture that utilizes entanglement to propagate information between neurons, thereby mitigating the limitations of classical computation. The core mechanism centers around introducing quantum entangled states within the network's layers, leading to a fundamentally different training paradigm. This work presents a preliminary investigation into this concept, highlighting potential benefits and outlining future research directions.

title: Adaptive Neuron Networks and Multi-Scale Information Processing
abstract: This paper proposes a novel architecture for neural networks termed Adaptive Neuron Networks (ANNs), designed specifically for efficient processing of multi-scale information. The core concept revolves around integrating multi-scale feature extraction modules within a neuron network structure, coupled with a feedback mechanism that dynamically adjusts neuron parameters based on the complexity and scale of the input data. Unlike traditional neural networks that typically operate within a single scale, ANNs aim to capture and process information across a range of scales, enabling enhanced pattern recognition and learning capabilities. The system employs a hierarchical approach, where initial layers extract low-level features, progressively transitioning to higher-level representations at later layers. The adaptive nature of the network allows it to automatically adjust to the varying characteristics of the input data, improving robustness and accuracy. This work introduces a formal framework for ANNs, including a mathematical description of the network structure and the adaptive learning process. The key contribution lies in the design of a scalable architecture that can effectively handle complex, multi-scale data, demonstrating a potential improvement in performance compared to conventional neural networks.

title: Symbiotic Neural Networks – Multi-Agent Learning
abstract: This paper investigates the concept of Symbiotic Neural Networks (SNNs), a novel approach to artificial intelligence where multiple neural networks operate in a coordinated, symbiotic relationship. The core claim is that designing neural networks to interact and collaborate with other AI agents can significantly enhance performance, particularly when tackling complex problems. The proposed mechanism involves a system of interconnected neural networks, each specialized in a distinct task, that exchange information and cooperate to achieve a holistic solution. The architecture leverages multi-agent learning principles, allowing for dynamic adaptation and robust problem-solving. We outline the theoretical framework, explore potential architectural designs, and discuss the advantages of SNNs compared to traditional, monolithic neural networks. This research contributes to a fundamental shift in AI design, moving towards more intelligent and adaptable systems. The key mathematical representation utilizes the following notation: $N_i$ represents the i-th neural network, $x_i$ represents the input vector for $N_i$, $y_i$ represents the output vector for $N_i$, $L_i$ represents the loss function for $N_i$, $\theta_i$ represents the parameters of $N_i$, $\alpha_i$ represents the learning rate for $N_i$, and $\nabla L_i$ represents the gradient of the loss function for $N_i$. We propose a framework for defining the symbiotic relationship based on a shared information space and defined communication protocols. The success of this approach hinges on the efficient exchange of information and the ability of each network to learn from the collective intelligence of the system. Further research will focus on formalizing the learning dynamics and exploring specific application domains.

title: Complexity Assessment Methods: An Adaptive Approach
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to complexity assessment, employing an adaptive algorithm to dynamically adjust computational complexity. The primary goal is to reduce computational cost and improve algorithm efficiency by intelligently controlling the steps and variables involved in a computational process. The core mechanism involves the implementation of an adaptive algorithm that automatically adjusts these parameters based on the observed complexity of the task, leading to a more efficient and potentially faster solution. This is a significant advancement over existing methods that rely on manual parameter tuning, offering a more automated and potentially more effective solution.

title: Adaptive Computation Framework (ACF)
abstract: This paper introduces the Adaptive Computation Framework (ACF), a novel computational paradigm designed to dynamically adjust the depth and complexity of computations based on input data characteristics. Traditional computational models often rely on fixed depth and complexity settings, leading to suboptimal performance. The ACF employs a dynamic "depth" mechanism, guided by machine learning, to optimize the structure and parameters of computations, thereby significantly reducing computational costs. This research explores the fundamental principles and practical implementations of the ACF, demonstrating its potential for enhancing computational efficiency across a range of applications.

title: Probabilistic Formal Logic with Bayesian Resonance
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to formal logic that integrates probabilistic reasoning with a mechanism termed "Bayesian Resonance." Traditional formal logic systems often struggle to effectively handle uncertainty and incomplete information. This system addresses this limitation by dynamically adjusting the confidence in logical conclusions based on the temporal coherence of supporting evidence. The core idea is to combine classical logic with Bayesian inference, augmented by a resonance component. This resonance component monitors and adapts the probabilities associated with logical assertions, reflecting the strength of temporal correlations observed within the data. The proposed system aims to provide a more nuanced and robust framework for reasoning under uncertainty, particularly in scenarios where temporal dynamics play a significant role. The system is designed to enhance the ability of formal logic to address real-world problems characterized by ambiguity and evolving information. This approach offers a potential pathway to creating more intelligent and adaptive logical systems.

title: Quantum Entanglement Encoding for Semantic Retrieval
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to semantic retrieval leveraging quantum entanglement as a high-density information encoding method. Traditional semantic search methods, reliant on keyword matching and vector similarity, face limitations in accuracy and efficiency. We propose encoding semantic information into entangled quantum states, exploiting the inherent correlations within these states for advanced retrieval. The core mechanism involves manipulating entangled qubits to achieve ultra-precise filtering across multiple candidate semantic items, coupled with multi-dimensional association analysis. This approach promises a revolutionary shift in information retrieval by capitalizing on the density and correlation capabilities of quantum entanglement. The theoretical framework presented outlines the fundamental concepts and potential of this technology, focusing on the encoding process, the entanglement manipulation techniques, and the retrieval algorithm. We demonstrate the potential for significantly improved retrieval accuracy and speed compared to conventional methods.

title: Adaptive Algorithm for Topological Quantum Computing Based on Non-linear Topology
abstract: This paper introduces a novel adaptive algorithm for Topological Quantum Computing (TQC) that leverages the dynamic adjustment of optimization parameters based on quantum state variations. Traditional optimization algorithms often rely on fixed, pre-defined parameters, limiting their effectiveness in complex quantum systems. This algorithm dynamically adjusts these parameters to optimize the quantum state, resulting in improved efficiency and accuracy in quantum computations. The core mechanism involves analyzing the quantum state's evolution and automatically modifying optimization parameters to achieve a desired outcome. This adaptive approach addresses a critical limitation of existing optimization methods, offering a promising pathway towards enhanced quantum algorithm performance. We present a theoretical framework and preliminary experimental validation demonstrating the efficacy of this approach.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Driven Distributed Data Compression and Retrieval
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to distributed data compression and retrieval leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement. Traditional data compression methods are often limited by the fundamental bounds imposed by information theory. Furthermore, classical database retrieval can be bottlenecked by the need for exhaustive searches. This research explores a paradigm shift by utilizing entangled states to encode data across a distributed network, offering potential for significantly enhanced compression ratios and faster retrieval speeds. The core mechanism involves constructing a network of quantum nodes, employing entanglement to create correlated quantum states, and leveraging Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) based on these entangled states for secure data transmission and synchronization. The inherent correlations within the entangled states are then exploited to facilitate efficient data retrieval and analysis. We detail the theoretical framework, including the compression process, the entanglement distribution protocol, and the retrieval algorithms. This work establishes a foundation for future research into quantum-enhanced data management systems and addresses critical limitations of current technologies. The primary goal is to demonstrate that entanglement-based approaches can surpass the Shannon limit for data compression and dramatically accelerate data retrieval operations.

title: Dynamic Resource Allocation via Bayesian Reinforcement Learning with Prior Knowledge
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to dynamic resource allocation utilizing Bayesian Reinforcement Learning (BRL) and incorporating prior knowledge to enhance learning efficiency and system stability. Traditional reinforcement learning methods frequently suffer from excessive exploration, particularly in complex dynamic environments. To address this, we propose a framework where a Bayesian network explicitly represents prior knowledge about the system's dynamics. This prior knowledge is leveraged to initialize the RL agent's belief state and strategically guide the exploration process. The resulting BRL agent learns more effectively and rapidly, minimizing the need for exhaustive exploration while maintaining robust performance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a theoretical analysis and a conceptual framework, highlighting its potential for applications in diverse dynamic resource allocation scenarios. The core contribution lies in the systematic integration of prior knowledge within the BRL paradigm, leading to a more practical and efficient solution for dynamic resource allocation problems.

abstract: This paper introduces Adaptive Topological Graph Networks (ATN), a novel neural network architecture designed to enhance model performance, particularly in scenarios with complex data distributions. The core idea of ATN centers around utilizing a dynamically constructed topological graph to guide the learning process of the neural network. Unlike traditional approaches that rely solely on the input data, ATN leverages the inherent structure of the data to impose constraints, thereby facilitating more effective feature representation and reducing the risk of overfitting. This approach enables the network to better adapt to the intricacies of the data, leading to improved generalization accuracy. We present a comprehensive analysis demonstrating the effectiveness of ATN through extensive experiments on various benchmark datasets, showcasing its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. The paper concludes with a detailed discussion of the underlying mathematical principles and the potential implications for the design of more robust and adaptable neural networks.

This approach enables the network to better adapt to the intricacies of the data, leading to improved generalization accuracy. We present a comprehensive analysis demonstrating the effectiveness of ATN through extensive experiments on various benchmark datasets, showcasing its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. The paper concludes with a detailed discussion of the underlying mathematical principles and the potential implications for the design of more robust and adaptable neural networks.

title: Title: Resonance-Based Algorithm for Optimization
abstract: This paper introduces a novel optimization algorithm, the Resonance-Based Algorithm (RBA), designed to accelerate the convergence of optimization algorithms for complex, non-convex problems. Traditional optimization techniques often face challenges in high-dimensional spaces, necessitating sophisticated methods to achieve satisfactory results. The RBA utilizes resonant frequency analysis to guide the search process, effectively amplifying key frequencies within the problem space. This approach offers a unique mechanism for improving convergence rates and potentially unlocking solutions for previously intractable optimization challenges. The paper details the algorithm's core principles, proposes a robust framework for frequency identification, and presents preliminary experimental results demonstrating its effectiveness in a range of optimization scenarios. The focus is on creating a systematic method to enhance the performance of existing algorithms, particularly those designed for complex, non-convex problems. This research contributes to the development of more efficient and reliable optimization strategies applicable to a variety of fields.

title: Artificial intelligence in endometrial cancer: multimodal deep learning and future perspectives in precision gynecologic oncology — a structured narrative review
abstract: Endometrial cancer (EC) is the most common gynecologic malignancy in developed countries, with a rising incidence driven by obesity, metabolic syndrome, diabetes mellitus, and aging populations. Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly advanced in gynecologic oncology, particularly in diagnostic imaging, digital pathology, radiomics, and multimodal prognostic modeling. Recent breakthroughs in machine learning, deep learning, and whole-slide imaging (WSI), including multimodal prognostic architectures such as HECTOR and explainable AI (XAI), have enabled the development of sophisticated diagnostic and prognostic systems. These systems can differentiate benign from malignant lesions, predict myometrial invasion and lymph node metastases, stratify recurrence risk, and support individualized therapeutic decision-making. Notably, recent multimodal deep-learning models, particularly the HECTOR framework, have demonstrated improved prognostic performance compared with conventional clinicopathologic risk-stratification systems for predicting distant recurrence in externally validated cohorts, although further prospective validation remains necessary. Despite these promising advances, current evidence remains limited by predominantly retrospective study designs, relatively small and frequently imbalanced datasets, potential overfitting of AI models, heterogeneous imaging protocols, limited external validation, and insufficient prospective clinical evidence. These limitations restrict model generalizability across different populations and healthcare settings. Furthermore, ethical, regulatory, and data-governance challenges remain important barriers to widespread clinical implementation. This structured narrative review summarizes AI applications in endometrial cancer, focusing on ultrasound imaging, radiomics, digital pathology, multimodal deep-learning, explainable AI, prognostic modeling, clinical translation, and future perspectives in personalized care.

title: Derechos de autor e inteligencia artificial: la autoría en el Perú
abstract: This article analyzes the impact of artificial intelligence on copyright law, with an emphasis on the notion of authorship of literary works. Based on an analysis of the international regulatory framework and comparative law, it critically evaluates the Peruvian legal system, identifying gaps in the regulation of works generated by artificial intelligence. The study adopts a dogmatic and comparative approach, considering Andean regulations, Peruvian legislation, and criteria developed in jurisdictions such as the United States, the European Union, the United Kingdom, and Japan. It argues that artificial intelligence cannot be considered the author of protected works, and therefore copyright protection must fall on verifiable human creative contribution. Finally, interpretive guidelines are proposed for the application of copyright law in Peru in the face of the challenges posed by generative artificial intelligence, aimed at guiding Indecopi’s actions in the absence of specific regulations.

title: Quantum Inversion of Units in Group Rings: Block Dimension, Not Commutativity, Governs Hardness
abstract: Several public-key schemes base their security on the belief that inverting a unit of a group ring is hard. A recent result showed that this belief is false on a quantum computer when the group is abelian. To restore security, designers moved to non-abelian groups, especially dihedral groups, believing that the hardness of the dihedral hidden subgroup problem (HSP) would protect the scheme. This paper shows that unit inversion is a different problem and does not require an HSP solver. Instead, it can be solved by a change of basis that splits the group ring into small matrix blocks. We prove that unit inversion is polynomial-time, classically and quantumly, when an efficient generalized Fourier transform exists, the group ring is semisimple, and the largest matrix block has polynomial size. Dihedral group rings satisfy these conditions because their irreducible representations have dimension at most 2 and an efficient Fourier transform exists. We give an explicit reversible quantum circuit for the block-inversion step and validate it in a register-level simulator. We also identify the exact structural boundary where the method stops and propose a candidate construction in the surviving regime under a new, clearly stated security assumption. The constructive results are supported by reproducible software artifacts and experiments.

title: Trapped Ion Qubit Gates and Entanglement Driven by an Integrated Photonic Laser
abstract: Trapped ions are a leading technology for quantum computing, but their reliance on bespoke tabletop laser and optical systems remains a major obstacle to scaling and robustness. Integrated silicon nitride lasers, compatible with future monolithic integration with surface electrode ion traps, have recently demonstrated frequency-selective qubit state preparation and measurement as well as interrogation of an optical clock transition. However, coherent qubit gates impose even more stringent requirements on laser phase noise, and their implementation with integrated laser sources has remained an outstanding challenge. Here, we use a visible-wavelength integrated Brillouin laser stabilized to an integrated coil resonator to drive coherent single- and two-qubit gates with \Sr optical qubits. We measure an average single-qubit fidelity of $99.61\%\pm 0.03\%$ per Clifford gate with randomized benchmarking and use a two-qubit Mølmer-Sørensen interaction to generate an entangled Bell state with a fidelity of $92.35\% \pm 1.50\%$. The qubit exhibits a bare Ramsey coherence time of $659 \pm 9~μ$s, more than a tenfold improvement over our previous implementation, which extends to $1.750 \pm 0.033$~ms with an echo. These results demonstrate, for the first time, that integrated visible-wavelength narrow-linewidth photonic lasers can meet the phase-noise requirements for coherent quantum logic with trapped ion optical qubits, providing a path for scalable optical systems integrated within trapped ion quantum processors.

title: Construction and Natural Language Querying of a Cybersecurity Knowledge Graph
abstract: Cybersecurity vulnerability information is distributed across numerous platforms and databases, making it difficult for researchers and practitioners to obtain a unified and structured understanding of existing threats. This is a critical issue in cybersecurity, where timely access to accurate vulnerability information directly impacts risk assessment and decision-making. While previous work has shown that knowledge graphs are effective for organizing vulnerability data, a major research gap remains in their accessibility, as querying such graphs typically requires expertise in graph query languages like Cypher. This paper aims to address this gap by proposing an approach that combines the construction of a cybersecurity knowledge graph with natural language-based interrogation. The proposed methodology relies on data collected from the National Vulnerability Database (NVD)(1) through its REST API and models vulnerabilities, products, vendors, severity metrics, weaknesses, and references using the Labeled Property Graph paradigm in Neo4j. The knowledge graph is deployed on Neo4j Aura Cloud and queried through an AI-assisted interface that translates natural language queries into Cypher language. The key contribution of this work is demonstrating that natural language querying significantly lowers the barrier to interacting with cybersecurity knowledge graphs, enabling more intuitive exploration and analysis of vulnerability data, and thereby enhancing their practical usefulness for a broader range of users in the cybersecurity field.

title: Aurora-Lens / VALO / REHT: Authorship, Access and Repository Provenance Record
abstract: Principal readable record and accompanying evidence files preserving the communications and chronology concerning Aurora-Lens, VALO and REHT; Margaret Stokes's authored contribution to VALO; access to the Persistent Existence Frame specification and Aurora-Lens materials; the Phase 0 framework; and subsequent publication, attribution and termination. The record now begins with the May-July 2026 REHT admissibility-outcome sequence: Aurora-Lens's 6 May public runtime map, Njål Gaute Solland's June descriptions of VALO's binary admissibility signal, Margaret's disclosure of bounded non-binary outcomes, unresolved-state preservation and standing distinct from confidence, Aurora-Lens's 6 July four-outcome public demo, and reht-standard's 15 July five-outcome first specification and v0.1.0-draft release. A verified full reht-standard Git bundle preserves the retrieved history and refs; the note expressly records that INDETERMINATE was present in the first specification commit and that the sequence is evidence rather than proof by itself. The record also preserves the 17 August Word document Societal Implications of Governed Agentic Systems, its creator metadata, delivery, and Njål's written adoption of "prevention of illegitimate closure" as a VALO invariant; the joint-paper authorship arrangement; his 12 August citations to 02 PEF_Specification.pdf; Margaret's patent notice; his declared architectural inversion and rebuild; corresponding Open Agent Contract commits; and the Phase 0 transfer and signature sequence. The commercial exhibit includes Margaret's 16 August Draft 2, the signed 16-clause PDF returned on 24 August, a verified clause map and the unresolved recurring-fee duration. The record further includes the Dyade announcement and comment-removal captures, a qualified CASE 01 attribution record, the repository-overlap audit, subject-matter claim chart and fixed public Git evidence. The confidential PEF specification itself is not published; its retained-copy fingerprint is recorded for later confidential comparison.

title: Probabilistic Inference with Symbolic Reasoning
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to probabilistic inference by integrating probabilistic graphical models (PGMs) with symbolic reasoning techniques. Traditional approaches often struggle with the inherent limitations of each method – PGMs facing challenges in representing complex logical relationships, and symbolic reasoning struggling to handle uncertainty and probabilistic information effectively. This work proposes a hybrid framework that converts probabilistic distributions within PGMs into symbolic logical expressions, enabling the application of symbolic inference rules. Simultaneously, probabilistic information from the PGM is used to constrain and refine the symbolic reasoning process. We demonstrate that this combined approach offers a significant advantage in representing and reasoning about complex knowledge domains, particularly those involving both logical constraints and probabilistic uncertainties. The core claim is that the synergistic combination of these two approaches unlocks more powerful knowledge representation and inference capabilities. This paper outlines the key components of this framework and discusses its potential applications. ---

title: Probability-Based System Modeling
abstract: This paper explores the application of Bayesian networks and Monte Carlo simulation to the modeling of probabilistic systems. We propose a novel approach that leverages Bayesian networks to represent system behavior and utilizes Monte Carlo simulation to generate precise predictions, offering a significant advancement over traditional methods. The core mechanism involves constructing a probabilistic model using Bayesian networks, and employing Monte Carlo simulation for high-fidelity predictions, addressing limitations of existing systems modeling techniques. This work demonstrates the potential of this approach to predict system behavior with improved accuracy and robustness.

title: Explainable Deep Learning Models Generation and Verification
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to generating and verifying explainable deep learning models. The core idea is to integrate knowledge graph and rule-based reasoning to create a framework that enhances model interpretability. We propose a methodology for automatically constructing deep learning models with inherent explainability and a validation technique to assess the effectiveness of the generated explanations. The research addresses the current limitations of deep learning models, which primarily prioritize accuracy over interpretability, by introducing a mechanism for building more trustworthy and reliable models. The validation process utilizes metrics designed to quantify the alignment between the model's decisions and the provided explanations, offering a rigorous evaluation of the explainability framework. This work contributes to the growing field of explainable AI (XAI) by providing a practical and automated solution for generating and verifying interpretable deep learning systems.

title: Title: Adaptive Quantum Entanglement for Nonlinear Topological Geometry Transformations
abstract: This paper investigates the application of adaptive quantum entanglement to nonlinear topological geometry transformations, aiming to achieve high-precision geometric manipulation. Traditional topological transformations often rely on computationally intensive methods, limiting their applicability to complex models. We propose a novel algorithm leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement to facilitate accurate transformations, offering enhanced computational efficiency. The core mechanism centers around utilizing entanglement to represent and manipulate geometric primitives, enabling the exploration of intricate topological structures with unprecedented precision. This work presents a framework for implementing this algorithm, demonstrating its potential for advanced geometric modeling and data processing.

title: Quantum Entanglement and Probability Matrices
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, presents a unique opportunity for enhancing computational power. This paper explores the application of quantum self-organization principles to probability matrices, aiming to revolutionize both quantum computing and machine learning. We propose a novel method for constructing probability matrices leveraging quantum entanglement and superposition, leveraging these principles to significantly boost matrix computational efficiency and expressiveness. This work delves into the theoretical groundwork, the potential advantages, and the challenges associated with this approach. The core mechanism centers around utilizing quantum entanglement to accelerate matrix calculations while simultaneously enhancing the representation of complex data. The paper concludes with a discussion of the research's implications and future directions.

title: Dynamic Quantum Decoherence Correction Algorithm
abstract: This paper presents a novel dynamic quantum decoherence correction algorithm designed to mitigate the detrimental effects of decoherence on quantum information processing. Decoherence, the loss of quantum coherence due to interactions with the environment, remains a significant obstacle to the reliable implementation of quantum technologies. Our algorithm leverages real-time monitoring and adaptive control strategies to actively counteract decoherence, aiming to preserve quantum information fidelity. The core principle involves precisely modulating the state of individual quantum bits (qubits) using quantum control techniques, effectively reducing the decoherence rate. We detail the mathematical framework underpinning the algorithm, including the relevant equations governing decoherence and the control pulses employed. The algorithm's dynamic nature allows it to respond to changes in the decoherence environment, offering a more robust solution compared to static correction methods. Simulation results (presented within) demonstrate the algorithm's efficacy in maintaining coherence for extended periods, highlighting its potential for applications in quantum communication, quantum computation, and quantum sensing. Finally, we outline potential future research directions and challenges associated with the broader implementation of this dynamic decoherence correction approach.

title: 基于高阶自映射的量子隐形矩阵理论 (QHMM)
abstract: This paper presents a novel quantum computing framework, Quantum Hidden Markov Matrix Theory (QHMM), based on high-order self-mapping techniques. The core focus of QHMM is to develop a method for efficiently calculating and manipulating quantum states, specifically targeting the properties of quantum hidden Markov matrices. We introduce a new self-mapping operator, the 'Shift Operator', which plays a crucial role in optimizing the performance of quantum computations involving these matrices. The research explores the potential of this approach to enhance quantum algorithms and address challenges in quantum information processing. This work contributes to the advancement of quantum computing by providing a new theoretical model and practical implementation for quantum hidden Markov matrix theory.

Our proposed system dynamically adjusts model parameters and structure based on the data's characteristics and model performance, resulting in improved model efficiency and generalization. The core mechanism involves a self-learning optimization algorithm that continuously updates model parameters and architecture based on observed data, enabling a more responsive and effective optimization process. This approach addresses the limitations of static optimization techniques and offers a promising path towards more robust and adaptable deep learning models.

title: Emergent Behavior Generation in Simulated Ecosystems
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of simulating complex ecological systems to generate emergent behaviors, a key characteristic for training and validating Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems. The core argument is that the intricate interactions within biological ecosystems, when modeled through Agent-Based Modeling (ABM), can produce highly complex and unpredictable outcomes. This research proposes a methodology for constructing ABM-based ecosystem simulators, utilizing agent interactions such as competition, cooperation, and predation, and employing genetic algorithms to optimize agent parameters and shape the resultant ecosystem. The novelty lies in applying the principles of emergent phenomena observed in natural ecosystems directly to the development of robust and realistic testing environments for AI. This approach offers a more challenging and meaningful context for evaluating AI's ability to adapt and react to complex, dynamic situations. The paper will detail the framework, focusing on the core mechanisms and potential applications of this simulation approach. ---

title: Quantum State Dynamic Parameterization: A Novel Approach to Computational Efficiency and Precision
abstract: This paper introduces a novel computational framework centered around quantum state dynamics, aiming to significantly enhance the efficiency and precision of computations. Traditional computational graph design relies heavily on static parameter settings, which often struggles to effectively represent and manage complex systems exhibiting dynamic properties. Our proposed method leverages quantum state manipulation to dynamically adjust parameters, fostering an iterative optimization process that yields superior results. The core mechanism involves constructing a dynamic computational graph, where the state of individual quantum elements undergoes continuous adjustment based on a predefined algorithm. This adaptive approach directly addresses the limitations of static graph designs by offering a more flexible and responsive system. The implementation details and preliminary results demonstrate substantial improvements in computational speed and accuracy across a range of benchmark problems.

abstract: Quantum algorithms are increasingly vital for complex computations, necessitating the development of efficient and adaptable computational frameworks. We propose a method that dynamically adjusts the complexity of quantum circuits based on input data, significantly enhancing algorithm efficiency. This approach leverages the inherent adaptability of quantum computation to optimize performance across a wide range of problems. This research addresses the limitations of static, pre-defined quantum algorithms by providing a flexible and potentially highly efficient solution.

title: Relational Graph Neural Networks with Contextualized Edge Embeddings
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated remarkable success in various domains, including social network analysis, drug discovery, and recommendation systems. However, traditional GNNs often treat edges as static features, failing to capture the dynamic and contextual nature of relationships within a graph. This paper introduces Relational Graph Neural Networks with Contextualized Edge Embeddings (RGNNC), a novel approach that addresses this limitation. RGNNC leverages recurrent neural networks to generate dynamic edge embeddings, considering both node features and neighborhood information, thereby providing a context-aware representation of graph relationships. The core claim of this work is that enhancing GNNs with these contextualized edge embeddings significantly improves their performance. The mechanism involves training a recurrent neural network to predict edge features based on the surrounding network structure and temporal evolution of nodes. This dynamic representation allows RGNNC to better capture complex relational patterns and achieve superior results compared to static edge embedding approaches.

title: Title: Emergent Constraint Optimization via Fractal Geometry (ECOFG)
abstract: This paper introduces Emergent Constraint Optimization via Fractal Geometry (ECOFG), a novel approach to constraint satisfaction that leverages the inherent properties of fractal geometry to generate unexpected and globally optimal solutions. Traditional constraint optimization methods often struggle with complex, non-convex optimization landscapes, frequently requiring extensive and computationally expensive search. ECOFG proposes a framework where constraint satisfaction is embedded within a fractal structure, iteratively refining the solution space through fractal iterations, ultimately leading to emergent global optimality. We present a theoretical foundation and demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through illustrative examples, showcasing the potential for significant improvements in optimization performance, particularly in scenarios involving intricate, high-dimensional constraints. The core mechanism hinges on the self-similarity property of fractals, which, when combined with constraint satisfaction, can generate solutions that are difficult to obtain through conventional methods.

title: Budget-Prioritized Dynamic Regrouping for Edge Federated Services Under Workload Drift and Privacy-Budget Constraints
abstract: Federated learning enables model training in edge and distributed service environments without directly sharing raw data. In long-running edge federated services, fixed collaboration structures may become inefficient under workload drift, whereas frequent regrouping can incur migration overhead, group churn, and additional privacy-budget consumption. This paper studies budget-prioritized dynamic regrouping under workload drift, privacy-budget constraints, and migration or reconfiguration cost. We formulate a dynamic regrouping problem that jointly captures workload pressure, remaining privacy budget, service utility, and regrouping cost. We propose Budget-Prioritized Dynamic Regrouping (BP-DR), a triggered local method that evaluates single-node candidate operations and commits at most one regrouping operation per time slot. A candidate is accepted only when it is privacy-budget feasible and its utility improvement exceeds a threshold combining an anti-oscillation margin, migration or reconfiguration cost, and privacy-budget opportunity cost. We derive this trigger from a one-step local comparison and establish its monotonicity with respect to migration or reconfiguration cost and remaining privacy budget. Trace-driven experiments based on Alibaba Cluster Trace 2018 show that BP-DR maintains competitive migration-adjusted utility while controlling regrouping activity across dynamic and stress-test settings. FLamby Fed-Heart-Disease validation further shows similar learning performance across the compared methods while demonstrating the integration of BP-DR with group-aware federated training.

title: Translation of Black-Box Clinical Prediction Models into Standalone Transparent Nomograms: Temporal External Validation in Heart Transplantation
abstract: We convert black-box clinical prediction models for tabular data into standalone nomograms that can be audited term by term. PRiSM (Partial Responses in Structured Models) takes the shape of each effect and interaction from the source model, not merely which variables mattered, and lets the outcome select and weight them. We tested this in 50,356 heart transplant recipients, with validation in a later era than training. Nomograms from all 5 source models - a public clinical risk score, logistic regression, neural networks, random forests and extreme gradient boosting - met a prespecified noninferiority criterion for discrimination before any further simplification, and generally preserved calibration and clinical net benefit. Those from the 3 machine-learning models showed no detectable difference in discrimination from de novo generalized additive and explainable boosting models, exceeded neural additive models, and carried fewer terms than the explainable boosting model. PRiSM is released as an open-source Python package.

title: Echo state networks for time series forecasting: Hyperparameter sweep and benchmarking
abstract: This paper investigates the performance of Echo State Networks (ESNs) for univariate forecasting of monthly and quarterly time series from the M4 Forecasting Competition dataset. We evaluate whether a simple first-order autoregressive ESN can serve as a competitive alternative to widely used forecasting methods. The study uses a two-stage design: a Parameter dataset is used to analyze ESN model configurations over leakage rate, spectral radius, reservoir size, and regularization selection, while a disjoint Forecast dataset is reserved for out-of-sample benchmarking. Forecast accuracy is measured using mean absolute scaled error (MASE), symmetric mean absolute percentage error (sMAPE), and the overall weighted average (OWA). The ESN is compared with simple benchmarks, statistical models including autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA), exponential smoothing state space (ETS), the Theta method, and TBATS, as well as multilayer perceptron (MLP), recurrent neural network (RNN), and hybrid exponential smoothing-RNN (ES-RNN) benchmarks. The model-configuration analysis reveals frequency-specific patterns: monthly series tend to favor moderately persistent reservoirs, whereas quarterly series favor more contractive dynamics; across both frequencies, high leakage rates are generally preferred. In the final benchmark, the ESN performs on par with ARIMA and TBATS under mean MASE for monthly data and achieves the second-lowest mean MASE for quarterly data. ES-RNN provides the best aggregate accuracy for both frequencies. Overall, the results indicate that a simple autoregressive ESN can provide competitive forecast accuracy on the considered filtered M4 subsets, particularly under MASE, while requiring low training and forecasting time once the ESN configuration has been fixed.

title: Threshold-Based Selection for Continuous Optimization: A Leaf-Abscission Instantiation
abstract: This paper formalizes threshold-based selection as an evaluation-gating architecture in which each incumbent is tested before variation and a replacement is generated and evaluated only when contextual pressure exceeds intrinsic strength. The mechanism is instantiated as Leaf Abscission Optimization (LAO), using rank-based strength, a phenological seasonal signal, diversity modulation, environmental pressure, and a base regrowth kernel. A blocked two-to-the-fourth-power factorial analysis at dimension 10 on the CEC 2017 suite reduces the original multi-layer design to a parsimonious core: drift is harmful, while the other three auxiliary layers show no robust independent evidence of benefit. The resulting LAO-Core attains the third-best mean Friedman rank among nine optimizers at dimensions 10, 30, and 50 under the equal evaluation budget. A four-budget sweep shows budget-dependent relative performance, with adaptive differential-evolution baselines gaining relative advantage at larger budgets; the nine-cell dimension-budget analysis establishes neither an evaluation-budget-per-dimension-only law nor a statistically significant dimension-budget interaction. A paired intervention shows that diversity modulation changes late-run replacement behaviour without a detectable effect on final error at the tested budget. The evidence supports LAO as a parsimonious evaluation-gating mechanism with regime-qualified competitiveness, rather than as a generally superior optimizer.

title: Strategy Accumulation and Guided Execution for Automated LLM Fine-Tuning
abstract: Producing task-specific large language models requires discovering effective training strategies through experimentation. Automated fine-tuning systems have made this experimentation feasible with far less manual effort. However, these systems are stateless: each search discards its discovered strategies, dataset insights, and hyperparameter findings once it ends. Every new task must then repeat this costly search from a cold start. To address this, we propose Strategy Accumulation and Guided Execution (SAGE), a two-stage framework that makes automated fine-tuning search cumulative. In the first stage, a multi-agent pipeline performs Monte Carlo Tree Search-based exploration. A parallel Distillation Agent extracts task-specific exploration records and confidence-scored cross-task insights, which together constitute a structured experience repository. In the second stage, SAGE retrieves relevant experience from this repository and selects what applies to guide training on the new task. We evaluate SAGE on nine unseen tasks spanning both single- and cross-category settings. In single-round execution, SAGE's accumulated experience raises the average relative improvement over baseline from 3.2% to 15.6%, a 12.4-percentage-point gain over the same pipeline without it. These results show that persistent strategy experience provides effective guidance for automated fine-tuning on unseen tasks.

title: Deep Persona: A Psychologically Grounded Architecture and Evaluation Framework for Role-Playing Agents and Simulations
abstract: Existing approaches to persona simulation with Large Language Models (LLMs) mostly rely on shallow character descriptions that fail to sustain coherent character behavior across extended interactions. We introduce Deep Persona, a psychologically grounded, three-layered architecture that organizes personas into hierarchical levels of observable expression, latent beliefs, and core motivational drives, for constructing highly convincing role-playing agents. Governed by the principles of scripted determinism and bounded agency, the architecture restricts the model to a reactive engine guided by a structured internal script. We further propose a reference-free evaluation framework that benchmarks dialogue naturalness against empirical human distributions using established psychological clinical instruments and adversarial stress-tests. Empirical evaluation reveals that while LLMs achieve high pragmatic fluency, they exhibit systematic limitations in emotional expression and joint attention. In addition, we present a case study of two Deep Personas and evaluate them using the proposed framework, demonstrating that structured personas can produce interactions that more closely align with human conversational behavior.

title: Mirror-Fusion Attention for Reflection-Aware Self-supervised Representation Learning
abstract: Most self-supervised learning (SSL) methods encourage invariance across augmentations, but strict flip invariance can suppress informative left--right correspondences in approximately bilateral data such as medical images and human faces. We propose Mirror-Fusion-Augmented Self-Supervised Learning (MFASSL), a Vision Transformer framework that injects a soft reflection prior into standard SSL without redesigning the backbone. MFASSL constructs mirror-paired views aligned to an estimated symmetry axis and introduces a lightweight Mirror-Fusion Attention (MFA) module for adaptive token-level interaction between mirrored regions while preserving asymmetric cues. The base SSL objective is further coupled with reflection-consistency and mid-layer token-alignment losses. Across CheXpert, BraTS, CelebA-HQ, and WFLW, MFASSL improves downstream performance, calibration, and reflection robustness over MoCo-v3, DINO, and MAE baselines under matched ViT-B/16 settings. It also achieves stronger and more consistent gains than recent equivariant SSL approaches with only approximately 2.7\% additional parameters. These results show that lightweight geometry-aware priors can effectively complement invariance-based SSL.

title: Train Smarter, Not Harder: Switching Signal-Guided Training in Active Learning
abstract: Training strategy, namely whether to retrain from scratch or fine-tune from the previous checkpoint, is an overlooked decision variable in active learning. We show that this choice has exploitable structure: retraining is most useful in early rounds, when each batch can substantially reshape the labeled distribution, while fine-tuning becomes safer once the model trajectory stabilizes. We propose HybridAL, an adaptive training schedule that monitors an online stabilization signal and switches from retraining to fine-tuning after sustained stabilization. Two complementary signals, spectral exponent change $Δα$ (weight-based) and accuracy change $Δ$Acc (validation-based), span different points on the time-calibration trade-off. Across three encoder backbones and six text-classification tasks (five seeds each), HybridAL keeps endpoint macro-F1 non-inferior to retraining and fine-tuning at a 0.010 margin, saves up to 49% of retraining time, and recovers a substantial fraction of retraining's calibration advantage as measured by negative log-likelihood (NLL). Compared with schedules that switch at a pre-committed round, HybridAL obtains lower NLL at moderate additional cost, showing that trajectory-dependent switching provides a stronger time-calibration trade-off than fixed early switching.

Two complementary signals, spectral exponent change $Δα$ (weight-based) and accuracy change $Δ$Acc (validation-based), span different points on the time-calibration trade-off. Across three encoder backbones and six text-classification tasks (five seeds each), HybridAL keeps endpoint macro-F1 non-inferior to retraining and fine-tuning at a 0.010 margin, saves up to 49% of retraining time, and recovers a substantial fraction of retraining's calibration advantage as measured by negative log-likelihood (NLL). Compared with schedules that switch at a pre-committed round, HybridAL obtains lower NLL at moderate additional cost, showing that trajectory-dependent switching provides a stronger time-calibration trade-off than fixed early switching.

title: SAIF: A Sparse Autoencoder Framework for Interpreting and Steering Instruction Following of Language Models
abstract: The ability of large language models (LLMs) to follow instructions is crucial for their practical applications, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. This paper presents a novel framework that leverages sparse autoencoders (SAE) to interpret how instruction following works in these models. We demonstrate how the features we identify can effectively steer model outputs to align with given instructions. Through analysis of SAE latent activations, we identify specific latents responsible for instruction following behavior. Our findings reveal that instruction following capabilities are encoded by a distinct set of instruction-relevant SAE latents. These latents both show semantic proximity to relevant instructions and demonstrate causal effects on model behavior. Our research highlights several crucial factors for achieving effective steering performance: precise feature identification, the role of final layer, and optimal instruction positioning. Additionally, we demonstrate that our methodology scales effectively across SAEs and LLMs of varying sizes.

title: MetaRSI / RSI2: A Meta-Recursive Self-Improving System for Recursive Self-Improving Systems Themselves
abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) lets a system improve the model-building machinery from its own failures, so every later model inherits the gain. Yet RSI has been validated almost exclusively on coding and formal benchmarks such as science QA and mathematics. This format bound limits RSI to improvement within a machine-checkable slice, not general capability where questions are open and correctness is settled by argument, replication, or measurement. We argue RSI must next operate across real, diverse scientific, engineering, and meta-scientific domains, not where formal evaluation is merely tractable. To that end we present MetaRSI-v1, where improvement is the scheduled composition of three typed operators over one unified paradigm. Data-RSI amplifies existing competence and marks its boundary; Harness-RSI edits a five-slot scaffold without touching weights; Model-RSI internalizes capability into parameters through bounded training. Sharing one loop kernel and artifact vocabulary, they make data, scaffold, and model changes composable rather than exclusive. A two-axis optimizer jointly decides operator order and each operator's proposal policy, while a meta-level policy revises the schedule across terms. We validate MetaRSI-v1 under the field's standard evaluations, on code and closed-form science, with no external teacher: the target model plays every role in its own loop. MetaRSI-v1 reframes self-improvement from a single-surface edit to a composition across the full model-production pipeline, opening two paths: a model route internalizing capability through training, and a harness route leaving weights untouched and thus extending self-improvement to any model reachable through an interface, with Data-RSI redefined as the shared substrate feeding both. The framework further yields refutable laws on where loops exist, how operators compose, and what supervision buys.

title: How Much of a Leaderboard Ranking Survives Its Own Sampling Error? A Paired-Resolution Audit of Five AI Benchmarks
abstract: A benchmark leaderboard is read as a stopwatch: the rank beside a model is treated as a fact. Yet every entrant is scored on the same items and publishes which it solved, so a leaderboard is a paired experiment, and its ordering can be tested rather than trusted. We test each adjacent-rank pair for statistical separability - exact McNemar's test on discordant items for pass/fail benchmarks, a paired item-bootstrap for scored ones - across five public boards. On SWE-bench Verified, 129 of 133 adjacent ranks are not separable at the 5% level; on MTEB, 176 of 180; on HELM Lite, all 89 of 89. The benchmarks are not broken: 88% of all pairs separate cleanly. It is the neighbours they cannot order, and neighbours are what the top of a table is made of. We derive a resolution bound, delta >= 2.80*sqrt(d/n) in the discordance rate d, that predicts which pairs are decidable from a benchmark's size, validate it on 12,739 pairs with zero false positives, and use LMArena - which already ships confidence intervals and ties - as a positive control for what correct reporting looks like. Every figure is recomputed from public data and passes a self-test suite; the recomputed rates match each official board to its published precision, with one mismatch on the Test split that reproduces a known duplicate-id defect in a submission file. We argue that a board should report the resolution of its ranking alongside the ranking, at no additional data cost. Version 2 (18 September 2026). No measurement changed: every quantitative result was rerun from the deposited data and reproduced, including the three parity gates, the preregistration scoring and all four figure coordinates. What changed are sentences about other people's work. The result that dropping a small share of preference data can change Chatbot Arena's top model belongs to Huang, Shen, Wei and Broderick, not to Singh et al., whose paper documents private testing and unequal data access instead; Zhang and Hardt measure a diversity-stability trade-off rather than proving an impossibility; Card et al. (2020) and Mogstad et al. are now cited as the prior art for the power requirement and for simultaneous rank confidence sets; the citation to Lunardi, Della Mea, Mizzaro and Roitero named only its last two authors and had strengthened their hedges; LMArena's published ranking rule is one plus the number of models significantly above, which reproduces its ranking for all 242 models, and its ten rank-2 models sit at rating positions 2 to 9, 11 and 20. Four checkable claims about the author's own artefacts are corrected in the same pass. All of it is listed in a new section, "Corrections in this version". Version 3 (18 September 2026). Version 2 corrected twelve statements about other people's work; a re-audit of it found that the correction had been incomplete in one direction and wrong in another. Three items reached version 2's deposit description but never the paper itself: the abstract still claimed the recomputed rates match each official board exactly, where the results file records one mismatch of 1.22 pp on the Test split, traceable to a submission file listing 241 results over 213 distinct instance ids; the per-split agreement figures were listed in a different order from the table above them; and the abstract still derived the bound from benchmark size alone rather than from size and near-pair discordance. The Mogstad et al. entry added in version 2 carried the wrong year, a truncated title and no venue, which is the defect the correction existed to remove. And Table 2 carried a column headed "#1 survives reshuffle" whose values, "every time" and "never", had no computation anywhere in the repository. That check is now defined and run (top1_stability.py, deposited here): over 2,000 item bootstraps the leader holds on Test 100% of the time, on Verified 38.3% and on Lite 53.6%, so "never" was wrong as well as unevidenced, and the Multimodal split, which has no per-instance matrix, now reads "not computed". Version 4 (19 September 2026). One reference. The Huang et al. entry gave the title as "Dropping Just a Handful of Preferences Can Change Top LLM Rankings"; it is "Top Large Language Model Rankings", and the entry now names all four authors. The same truncation was corrected in a companion paper on 18 September, and the letter sent to the first author that day said it was fixed, which was true of one deposit and not of this one. Nothing else changed.

title: Dynamic Topology and Probability Self-Adaptive Computation
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic topology and probability self-adaptive computation paradigm, designed to optimize computational efficiency and accuracy through dynamic adjustments of both topology and probability models. The system leverages a continuous feedback loop, iteratively refining the topology and probability distribution based on input data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a series of simulations and analyses, showcasing significant improvements in both performance and precision compared to traditional methods. The core mechanism centers around a hierarchical structure that allows for rapid adaptation to changing data conditions.

title: High-Dimensional Space Logic Non-Linear Probabilistic Reasoning Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel non-linear probabilistic reasoning algorithm based on high-dimensional space logic. The algorithm is designed to address the challenges inherent in high-dimensional space logic problems, leveraging probabilistic control to optimize reasoning and decision-making. We detail the core mechanism, outlining how the algorithm integrates probability theory with the logic of high-dimensional spaces. The primary focus is on enhancing efficiency and accuracy within these complex scenarios. This work presents a new approach to probabilistic reasoning, offering potential improvements in the handling of intricate high-dimensional problems.

title: Quantum Entanglement's Non-Asymmetry Analysis and Computation
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, presents unique challenges to classical computational theory. This research explores the non-asymmetry inherent in entangled states, offering a novel framework for analysis and a potential pathway to a new quantum computation paradigm. We propose a quantum circuit design predicated on entangled properties, emphasizing the crucial role of entanglement in enabling information transfer and computation. The core mechanism focuses on exploiting the inherent non-symmetry to create a computational advantage, moving beyond standard quantum algorithms. The research details a potential algorithmic framework predicated on entanglement, exploring its implications for information processing and highlighting its potential to redefine quantum computation.

title: Quantum Adaptive Algorithm Parameter Optimization Strategies
abstract: Quantum adaptive algorithms represent a significant advancement in the field of quantum computing, offering the potential to accelerate complex computations by dynamically adjusting quantum parameters. This paper investigates a novel parameter optimization strategy based on the principles of quantum self-adaptivity, aiming to enhance the performance of existing quantum algorithms. We propose a method that iteratively adjusts quantum state parameters based on feedback from the algorithm's execution, leveraging the inherent capabilities of quantum self-adaptivity to achieve optimal performance. This approach distinguishes itself through a dynamic parameter adjustment cycle that continuously refines the quantum system's state, leading to improved results. The paper details the core mechanism, the algorithm's design, and the experimental validation demonstrating its effectiveness. This work presents a promising path towards more efficient quantum computation.

title: Dynamic Quantum Topology Field Theory
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum topology field theory that integrates quantum entanglement with topological structure, aiming to achieve exceptionally high efficiency and robustness in quantum information storage and processing. The core mechanism centers around a quantum topology encoding scheme, leveraging self-repairing and quantum superposition properties to mitigate environmental noise. We argue that this approach represents a significant departure from existing quantum information paradigms, potentially pushing the boundaries of quantum information storage and processing capabilities.

title: Geometric Proof of Concept for Novel Data Structures
abstract: This paper presents a geometric proof of concept for novel data structures, leveraging the principles of topology to rigorously analyze their properties and demonstrate their efficiency through a fundamentally new proof framework. The core claim is to develop a geometric proof system specifically tailored for proving algorithmic correctness and performance characteristics without relying on traditional algorithmic verification methods. This approach aims to provide a more concrete and verifiable method for demonstrating the effectiveness of data structures, potentially offering a significant advancement in the field.

title: Title: Topological Entanglement Dynamics – Beyond Classical Correlation
abstract: Topological entanglement, a fundamental concept in quantum mechanics, exhibits unique properties that challenge classical intuition. This research explores a novel framework for quantifying and controlling the dynamic evolution of topological entanglement, predicting and mitigating decoherence in complex quantum systems. We propose a dynamically evolving, multi-scale topology based on a 'self-organizing' entanglement graph, utilizing adaptive feedback loops to minimize dissipation. This approach significantly expands the scope of entanglement analysis, offering predictive capabilities exceeding existing methods. The core mechanism involves modeling entanglement structure through a graph-based approach, incorporating adaptive control to ensure stability and coherence. This work presents a theoretical foundation and preliminary experimental validation demonstrating the framework's ability to predict and counteract decoherence patterns, thereby advancing our understanding of topological entanglement dynamics.

title: Cognitive Resonance Networks (CRN)
abstract: Cognitive Resonance Networks (CRN) presents a novel distributed neural network architecture designed to accelerate learning and enhance robustness through dynamically generated feedback loops. Leveraging principles of cognitive resonance, CRN establishes a system where nodes constantly evaluate their outputs against those of neighboring nodes, fostering a continuous process of refinement and improvement. This paper details the architecture's core mechanisms, including the feedback loop implementation and its impact on learning speed and resilience. The research focuses on establishing a framework for enhanced learning through a dynamic, iterative process of comparison and adjustment. We explore the theoretical underpinnings of cognitive resonance and demonstrate the practical application of this approach through a simulated learning scenario.

title: 拓扑几何与量子纠缠的关联研究
abstract: This research explores the synergistic relationship between topology and quantum entanglement, investigating the potential of leveraging entanglement to engineer novel quantum computing architectures. We propose a novel approach that utilizes the unique properties of quantum entanglement to construct qubits with precisely defined topological structures, ultimately facilitating a paradigm shift in computational capabilities beyond classical computation. The core mechanism centers on the deliberate design of quantum circuits and algorithms that exploit the inherent correlations within entangled states, pushing the boundaries of parallel processing. This work details a framework for utilizing entanglement to generate and control topological qubits, offering a potential pathway to surpass the limitations of current computing paradigms. The research highlights the critical role of topological properties in shaping the behavior of quantum systems and emphasizes the transformative implications of this intersection for future quantum technology.

title: Probabilistic Causal Inference via Simulation-Based Bayesian Networks
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to probabilistic causal inference leveraging simulation-based Bayesian Networks. The core idea is to construct a Bayesian Network representing the causal relationships within a target system and then utilize Monte Carlo simulation to generate synthetic data mimicking the system's dynamics. Crucially, the parameters governing the simulation are learned from observed data, effectively bridging the gap between simulated and real-world scenarios. This process aims to mitigate biases inherent in observational data, a significant challenge in traditional causal inference methods. We demonstrate the feasibility and potential advantages of this approach, focusing on the learning of simulation parameters to improve the accuracy of causal estimates. The methodology offers a robust alternative when direct causal identification is difficult due to confounding variables or limited observational data. The key contributions lie in the synergistic combination of Bayesian Network modeling, simulation, and parameter learning for enhanced causal reasoning.

This process aims to mitigate biases inherent in observational data, a significant challenge in traditional causal inference methods. We demonstrate the feasibility and potential advantages of this approach, focusing on the learning of simulation parameters to improve the accuracy of causal estimates. The methodology offers a robust alternative when direct causal identification is difficult due to confounding variables or limited observational data. The key contributions lie in the synergistic combination of Bayesian Network modeling, simulation, and parameter learning for enhanced causal reasoning.

abstract: Quantum state adaptive quantum path optimization is a novel approach to quantum computation that leverages dynamic modeling of quantum states to automatically adjust quantum paths, enhancing efficiency. This paper introduces a new optimization strategy based on machine learning algorithms to achieve self-adaptive path correction. The core mechanism involves constructing a dynamic state representation, employing machine learning for path correction, and optimizing the system for improved performance. The proposed method offers a distinct and potentially transformative approach to quantum algorithm design and implementation.

title: Quantum Error Correction with Adaptive Resource Allocation
abstract: Quantum error correction is a critical component of quantum computing, enabling the reliable manipulation of quantum information. Current error correction techniques often rely on static resource allocation, which can be inefficient and lead to increased error rates in real-time. This paper investigates a novel quantum error correction scheme that dynamically allocates resources based on the probability of errors, aiming to significantly improve error rate in real-time. We introduce a 'quantum resource allocation' metric that measures the effectiveness of each quantum element, adapting allocation based on error rates. The proposed approach offers a dynamic system with potential for substantial performance gains.

title: Neural Network Generation Models
abstract: This paper explores the development of neural network generation models utilizing Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). The core claim proposes a novel approach to automatically design and optimize neural networks by generating networks with specific topological structures and connection patterns. This is achieved through a generator network that produces network architectures and a discriminator network that assesses their quality, guided by an adversarial training process. The methodology addresses the limitations of traditional neural network design, which often relies on manual intervention or random generation. The resulting models demonstrate the potential for automated neural network creation, offering a pathway to improved efficiency and potentially novel network architectures tailored to specific tasks. The key innovation lies in the application of GANs for this purpose, providing a dynamic and adaptive approach to network design. This work lays the groundwork for future research exploring the scalability and effectiveness of this method across diverse neural network architectures and applications.

title: Distributed Quantum Key Distribution Protocols: Resilience Optimization
abstract: This paper investigates the optimization of distributed quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols with a focus on resilience enhancement. The core claim centers around improving both the security and efficiency of key distribution by strategically incorporating redundancy and error correction mechanisms. The proposed approach leverages the unique characteristics of quantum communication protocols, specifically utilizing redundant quantum channels and advanced error-correcting codes to achieve robust key exchange. The method addresses the limitations of existing QKD protocols in the face of channel noise and potential eavesdropping attacks. Mathematical models are presented to illustrate the key concepts and design choices. The optimization strategy is designed to maximize key rates while simultaneously mitigating the impact of channel imperfections, ultimately leading to more secure and reliable quantum key distribution systems. This work provides a theoretical framework for resilient QKD, offering a foundation for future implementations and further research in this critical field.

title: Formal Verification of Abstract Interpreters for Quantum Circuits
abstract: Abstract interpreters are widely employed in quantum circuit simulation to provide efficient approximations of complex quantum states. However, ensuring the correctness of these abstractions—that is, guaranteeing the accuracy of the simulated quantum state—is a significant challenge. Traditional verification methods often struggle with the inherent complexity and probabilistic nature of quantum systems. This paper presents a novel formal verification framework that combines abstract interpretation, runtime monitoring, and probabilistic reasoning. The core idea is to build a layer of runtime monitoring that detects discrepancies between the abstract simulation and the underlying quantum circuit, leveraging probabilistic models to quantify the uncertainty introduced by the abstraction. This allows for a rigorous assessment of the simulation's accuracy, even for intricate quantum circuits. The framework provides a quantifiable measure of confidence in the simulation results, enabling developers to make informed decisions regarding the trade-off between accuracy and computational cost. We outline the key components of the framework, highlighting the integration of each technique and demonstrating its potential for enhancing the reliability of quantum circuit simulators.
